title: Consciousness and the science of the mind
stage: Graduate study and research in neuroscience
audience: a graduate preparing for research in neuroscience or cognitive science, or a graduate student in the first years of a PhD or a research role
purpose: Study the science of consciousness and its debates at graduate level: what needs explaining and the hard problem, measuring consciousness and its contents, contrastive methods and neural correlates, blindsight and neglect, the major theories (global workspace, higher-order, recurrent processing, integrated information and predictive processing), adversarial collaborations, consciousness in disorders of consciousness, anesthesia and sleep, and the questions about infants, animals and artificial systems, with each view presented in its strongest form.
primary_reading: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "The Neuroscience of Consciousness" (free online)

weeks.1: What needs explaining: the hard problem and the easy problems
weeks.2: Measuring consciousness: reports, no-report paradigms and confidence
weeks.9: Predictive processing and the free-energy principle
weeks.11: Disorders of consciousness, anesthesia and sleep

blocks.deliverable: Compute a metacognitive sensitivity measure from supplied data.
Evaluate a claim of unconscious perception.
State the predictions that separate two theories.
Week 7 midterm; compute a simple integration measure for a tiny system.
Design an experiment that pits two theories against each other.
Write a balanced analysis of consciousness in one non-human system.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Seminar paper: write a 5,000-word seminar paper that evaluates one theory of consciousness against the strongest evidence and objections, presents its main rival fairly, and proposes one experiment whose result would count against the theory you find more plausible.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
